questions.question_text: Which of these integrals can be found directly using $\int f'(x)e^{f(x)}\,dx = e^{f(x)} + C$?

options.why: Here $f'(x) = 4x^{3}+1$, and $x^{3}$ is not a constant multiple of it.
There is no factor of $f'(x) = 4x^{3}$ present at all.
The index and the factor are swapped: here $f'(x) = 12x^{2}$, not $x^{4}$.

questions.solution_text:
$\int 4x^{3}e^{x^{4}}\,dx$ has $f(x) = x^{4}$ and $f'(x) = 4x^{3}$, which is exactly the factor present.
$\int 4x^{3}e^{x^{4}}\,dx$
$= e^{x^{4}} + C$

questions.question_text: For which value of $k$ is $\int kxe^{2x^{2}+7}\,dx = e^{2x^{2}+7} + C$?

options.why: Used the coefficient of $x^{2}$ in the index instead of differentiating the index.
Divided by the inner derivative instead of matching it, inverting the required factor.
Assumed no factor is needed, as if $\int e^{f(x)}\,dx = e^{f(x)} + C$.

questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = 2x^{2}+7$, so $f'(x) = 4x$.
The primitive is $e^{f(x)} + C$ exactly when the factor is $f'(x)$.
$kx = 4x$
$k = 4$
